Corporatism

/KOR-per-uh-tiz-uhm/ - the stress falls on KOR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Corporatism means control of policy or society by organized interest groups, especially large corporations.

Historians describe the old guild republic as early corporatism: the weavers' and bankers' associations cast votes in the senate itself.

Worked Example

Look at who signs the fishing quotas. On the nine-member board that sets each season's limits, the trawler owners' association holds three seats by statute, and its staff writes the first draft of every rule the ministry later announces. The small day-boat crews, who own no association, read the finished quotas in the newspaper like everyone else.

Corporatism is the exact word for that arrangement, because corporatism means control of policy or society by organized interest groups, especially large corporations — the mark is the seat at the table. A lobbyist waits in the hallway and hopes; under corporatism the industry sits on the board, pen in hand, an organ of the very government it once had to persuade.

How Corporatism Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

cronyism

cronyism: favors flow to friends informally; corporatism seats the groups formally, by rule

insider rule

insider rule: the blunt everyday phrase for governance captured by those it governs

Antonyms

impartiality

impartiality: the state weighs every voice and favors no organized bloc

independence

independence: government kept free of the industries it referees

How Strong Is It? — lobbying → corporatism → oligarchy

lobbying vs. corporatism

lobbying vs. corporatism: Lobbying is the weakest grip — industries argue their case from the hallway, and the government can still shut the door.

oligarchy vs. corporatism

oligarchy vs. corporatism: Oligarchy goes further than corporatism — corporatist groups share the table with the state; an oligarchy's few interests own the table outright.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of corporatism.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — corporat

Root — corporat: formed into one body (Latin corpus, corporis — body)

Suffix — -ism

Suffix — -ism: system, doctrine

Put it together

Put it together: Corporat- (formed into a body) + -ism = the system of the organized bodies. Latin corpus is a body; a corporation is many people legally fused into one body, and corporatism is what you get when those bodies, not individual citizens, become the units the state actually listens to.

Use the root in a new word: incorporate

Use the root in a new word: incorporate: In- means into, so planners who incorporate a suggestion fold it into the body of the design — the same corpus at work.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / political

Corporatism is analysis-and-editorial vocabulary, and the test is formal standing: if organized industries hold actual seats, pens, or votes inside government, corporatism is the word. Cronyism is the informal cousin — favors without the furniture. Its unit-mates map the rest of the field: mercantilism is the state running trade, laissez-faire the state stepping back, consumerism the households buying.
